A copy of the notice must be served on the owner from 5 days before to 30 days after filing, by personal delivery, certified or registered mail, or the other methods § 11 allows. Proof of service must be filed with the county clerk within 35 days after the lien is filed, or the lien ends (§ 11).

The lien lasts 1 year after filing. To keep it, the lienor must start a foreclosure action and file a notice of pendency within that year, or extend the lien (§ 17). On most projects one extension can be filed with the clerk; liens on single-family dwellings can be extended only by court order. Extension rules are technical, so confirm with counsel before relying on one.

A lien that is willfully exaggerated is void (§ 39). The lienor can then owe the owner or contractor the cost of discharging the lien, reasonable attorney fees, and the amount of the exaggeration (§ 39-a).

penalty_details: Knowingly filing a claim of lien that is not authorized by statute, or filing one to hinder, harass, or wrongfully interfere with someone, is a Class I felony (§ 44A-12.1). In lien suits the court may also award reasonable attorney fees to the prevailing party (§ 44A-35, amended 2022).
notes: Notice to Lien Agent generally required on projects with a designated lien agent; best practice to send within 15 days of first furnishing for full protection. Claim of Lien on Real Property must be filed and served within 120 days after last furnishing; enforcement action/lis pendens within 180 days of last furnishing.
public_notes:
North Carolina's lien law is in Chapter 44A, Article 2. On many private projects the owner must name a lien agent: generally where the improvement costs $40,000 or more, except work on an existing single-family home the owner lives in (G.S. 44A-11.1). On those projects, a claimant should get a Notice to Lien Agent to the lien agent within 15 days after first furnishing labor or materials (G.S. 44A-11.2). A later notice still works only if it arrives before a sale of the property to a good-faith buyer is recorded, and the lien can lose priority to loans recorded before the notice. Whether a contractor hired directly by the owner also needs to send this notice is debated in secondary sources, so confirm with counsel; most practitioners send it.

A claim of lien must be filed in the office of the clerk of superior court in each county where the property sits, no later than 120 days after the claimant's last furnishing (G.S. 44A-12). It must be served as G.S. 44A-11 requires. It cannot be amended, only cancelled and refiled within the 120 days.

The suit to enforce the lien must be filed within 180 days after last furnishing (G.S. 44A-13), which can leave as little as 60 days after the lien is filed.

Knowingly filing a lien that no statute authorizes, or filing one to harass or wrongfully interfere with someone, is a Class I felony (G.S. 44A-12.1). The court may award reasonable attorney fees to the prevailing party in a lien suit (G.S. 44A-35).

penalty_details: An owner who successfully contests the validity or accuracy of a construction lien in district court must be awarded all costs and reasonable attorney fees (§ 35-27-24.1). No lien exists for any amount if the claimant knowingly demanded more than is justly due (§ 35-27-16). The former criminal penalty section (§ 35-27-26) was repealed in 2009.
notes: Pre-lien notice: send owner certified-mail notice at least 10 days before recording the lien (N.D.C.C. §35-27-02). Record lien within 90 days after contribution is done; lien statement includes first/last contribution dates; absolute cap: not more than 3 years after first material is furnished (N.D.C.C. §35-27-13). Pre-suit enforcement notice: 10 days (personal) or 20 days (registered mail) before suit (N.D.C.C. §35-27-24). Owner demand can accelerate: suit + lis pendens within 30 days or lien forfeited; also suit+lis pendens must occur within 3 years after lien recording (N.D.C.C. §35-27-25). Tenant work: no lien unless owner has notice and fails to object (N.D.C.C. §35-27-07(3)).
public_notes:
North Dakota construction liens are governed by Chapter 35-27 of the Century Code. No preliminary notice is required at the start of a job. Before recording a lien, the claimant must send the owner written notice that a lien will be claimed, by certified mail, at least 10 days before recording (N.D.C.C. 35-27-02). The statute places this sentence in the part of the section about claimants hired through a contractor or subcontractor, but sending it in every case is the safer course; confirm with counsel if you contracted directly with the owner.

The lien is recorded with the county recorder where the property sits, within 90 days after the claimant's work or materials are complete (35-27-13). It must state the amount due, the dates of first and last contribution, and who hired the claimant. A late lien is not void, but it loses to good-faith buyers and lenders whose rights arise first and to payments the owner already made, and no lien may be filed more than 3 years after first furnishing (35-27-14).

Before suing, the claimant must give the owner written notice of intent to enforce at least 10 days ahead by personal service or 20 days ahead by registered mail (35-27-24). Suit must be started and a lis pendens recorded within 3 years after the lien is recorded. If the owner delivers and records a written demand, the claimant has only 30 days (35-27-25).

A claimant who knowingly demands more than is due loses the lien (35-27-16). An owner who successfully contests a lien's validity or accuracy in district court must be awarded costs and reasonable attorney fees (35-27-24.1).

notes: Notice of Furnishing: for claimants without direct contract, when a Notice of Commencement is filed, serve Notice of Furnishing not later than 21 days after first furnishing; late notice limits lien to work/materials furnished within 21 days before service and thereafter (Ohio Rev. Code §1311.05). Lien filing (private): affidavit for mechanic’s lien generally within 75 days after last furnishing; for work on a one- or two-family dwelling, within 60 days after last furnishing (Ohio Rev. Code §1311.06(B)). Lien duration/enforcement: lien continues for 6 years from filing unless enforced/otherwise discharged (Ohio Rev. Code §1311.13). Tenant improvements: liens generally attach only if owner is deemed to have consented/authorized; treat as owner_consent_required in this sheet (see generally §1311.04).
public_notes:
Ohio mechanics liens are governed by Chapter 1311 of the Revised Code. When the owner records a notice of commencement, subcontractors and suppliers who are not hired directly by the owner must serve a notice of furnishing within 21 days after they first furnish labor or materials (R.C. 1311.05). Late notice protects only work furnished in the 21 days before service and afterward. The notice is not required on improvements made under a home construction contract, and some one- and two-family projects with multiple original contractors are also exempt; confirm with counsel on residential jobs.

The lien affidavit is filed with the county recorder where the property is located. The deadline runs from the last day labor or materials were furnished: 60 days for a one- or two-family dwelling or a residential condominium unit, 75 days for most other projects, and 120 days for oil and gas well work (R.C. 1311.06). The affidavit is sworn before a notary or other officer who can give oaths. Within 30 days after filing, the claimant must serve a copy on the owner; if that cannot be done, the copy may be posted on the property within the next 10 days (R.C. 1311.07).

A lien lasts 6 years after the affidavit is filed, and longer if a suit to enforce it is pending (R.C. 1311.13). An owner can shorten this by serving a notice to commence suit; the lienholder then has 60 days to sue or the lien is void (R.C. 1311.11).

Chapter 1311 has no general penalty for an inflated lien, but owners may bring common-law claims. On home construction work, failing to release a paid lien within 30 days after written notice can make the lienholder liable for damages and attorney fees.

penalty_details: A claimant who falsifies the notarized pre-lien compliance affidavit filed with the lien commits a misdemeanor (fine up to $5,000, up to 30 days in jail) (§ 142.6(C)); an original contractor who falsifies a lien statement to the owner of a dwelling commits a felony (§ 142.4). In a lien enforcement action the party who wins judgment recovers a reasonable attorney fee (§ 176).
notes: Pre-lien notice: for claimants not in privity with owner (e.g., subs/suppliers), a pre-lien notice must be sent to the owner and original contractor within 75 days after last furnishing (for commercial/most projects) to preserve lien rights (42 O.S. §143.2(B)); residential/owner-occupied has stricter limits (see §143.1 and §143.2). This sheet captures 75-day notice as a prelim proxy. Lien filing deadline: original contractor within 4 months after last furnishing; all other claimants within 90 days after last furnishing (42 O.S. §142). Enforcement: suit must be brought within 1 year after filing the lien statement (42 O.S. §172). Owner-occupied/residential: subs/suppliers often have no lien rights absent direct contract or compliance with specific residential notice statutes; this row flags owner_occupied_restriction_type=direct_contract_only as a conservative rule and explains nuance in notes.
public_notes:
Oklahoma's mechanics lien law is in Title 42 of the statutes. A contractor or supplier who contracts directly with the owner must file a lien statement within 4 months after last furnishing labor, materials, or equipment (42 O.S. 142). Subcontractors, their suppliers, and lower tiers have 90 days after last furnishing (42 O.S. 143). The statement is filed with the county clerk where the land sits and must be verified by affidavit. The county clerk then mails notice of the lien to the owner by certified mail within 5 business days after filing (42 O.S. 143.1).

Claimants other than the original contractor must send a pre-lien notice to the original contractor and an owner before filing the lien, and no later than 75 days after the last date they furnished (42 O.S. 142.6). The notice is not required for claims under $10,000 or for residential projects of four or fewer units where no owner lives, but it is always required when an owner occupies the property as a dwelling. Certified mail, return receipt requested, creates a presumption that it was sent. When filing the lien, the claimant gives the clerk a notarized affidavit confirming the pre-lien notice was sent. Falsifying that affidavit is a misdemeanor. Work not covered by a required notice cannot be liened.

A suit to enforce the lien must be filed in district court within 1 year after the lien is filed (42 O.S. 172). The party who wins judgment in a lien suit recovers a reasonable attorney fee (42 O.S. 176). Special rules apply to owner-occupied homes, so confirm with counsel on residential jobs.

penalty_details: In a suit to foreclose, the court must award reasonable attorney fees at trial and on appeal to the party who prevails on the validity and foreclosure of the lien, so an owner who defeats a lien recovers fees. Levelset also says a baseless lien is a Class A misdemeanor; that statute was not located or read.
notes: Lien filing deadline: generally 75 days after completion of construction for residential construction (ORS 87.035(1)); 90 days after completion for nonresidential/commercial (ORS 87.035(1)). Completion is defined in ORS 87.005 and includes cessation/acceptance. Owner-occupied residential: most claimants not in direct contract must provide an 'Information Notice to Owner' within 8 days after starting work or delivering materials; certain professional services have 5-day timing (ORS 87.039). This sheet encodes 8 days as a general prelim proxy and flags enhanced_notice. Enforcement: suit must be commenced within 2 years after the lien is filed (ORS 87.055). Tenant improvements: lien generally attaches only if owner is an 'owner' under ORS 87.005 or has consent/agency; treat as owner_consent_required.
public_notes:
Oregon's Construction Lien Law is in ORS Chapter 87. A claimant who furnishes materials or labor without being hired by the owner generally must give the owner a notice of right to a lien (ORS 87.021). It can be sent at any time, but it protects only work furnished after a date 8 business days before the notice was delivered or mailed, so send it early. On commercial improvements, which include everything except an owner-occupied home of four or fewer units, claimants who provide labor, or labor and materials, or who rent equipment do not need this notice; material-only suppliers still do. On residential contracts over $2,000, the original contractor must give the owner an Information Notice to Owner or lose lien rights (ORS 87.093).

Most claimants must file the claim of lien no later than 75 days after they stop furnishing labor, equipment, or materials, or 75 days after construction is completed, whichever comes first, on commercial and residential work alike (ORS 87.035). The claim is recorded with the county recording officer and must be verified by oath. Within 20 days after filing, the claimant must mail notice of the filing, with a copy of the claim, to the owner and mortgagee, or lose fees and costs (ORS 87.039).

The lien expires 120 days after it is filed unless suit to foreclose is brought in that time (ORS 87.055). If the claim states extended payment terms, the period runs 120 days from the end of that credit, but never past 2 years after filing; confirm with counsel before relying on an extension. At least 10 days before suing, the claimant must give the owner and mortgagee written notice of intent to foreclose (ORS 87.057). The party who prevails on the lien recovers reasonable attorney fees (ORS 87.060).

notes: Lien filing: claim must be filed within 6 months after completion of the claimant’s work (49 P.S. §1502(a)(1)). Serve notice of filing of claim on owner within 1 month after filing (49 P.S. §1502(a)(2)). Enforcement: proceed by writ of scire facias within 2 years after filing claim (49 P.S. §1701). Owner-occupied residential exception: no lien by subcontractor against owner-occupied residential property (generally single family) unless subcontractor has a direct contract with the owner (49 P.S. §1303). PA also recognizes 'Notice of Commencement' concept for certain projects and allows contractual lien waivers in many contexts; not modeled here.
public_notes:
Pennsylvania's Mechanics' Lien Law of 1963 governs private construction liens. A claim must be more than $500. Contractors hired by the owner and subcontractors, including second-tier subcontractors and suppliers to a contractor or first-tier subcontractor, can file. Suppliers to a supplier cannot.

The claim is filed with the prothonotary of the court of common pleas where the property is located, within 6 months after the claimant completes its own work (Act 497, sections 201 and 502). Completion means the last labor or materials the claimant's contract required, so small punch-list work may not extend the date; confirm with counsel. A subcontractor must give the owner formal written notice of intention to file at least 30 days before filing (section 501). Within one month after filing, the claimant must serve notice of the filing on the owner, and must file an affidavit of service within 20 days after service, or the claim can be struck (section 502).

On projects costing $1.5 million or more where the owner has filed a notice of commencement in the State Construction Notices Directory, subcontractors must file a notice of furnishing there within 45 days after first furnishing (section 501.3). Subcontractors generally cannot lien a one- or two-family home or townhouse the owner lives in once the owner has paid the contractor in full (section 301).

An action on the claim must be started within 2 years after filing, unless the owner extends the time in writing, and judgment must be obtained within 5 years after filing (section 701). A claimant who fails to mark a paid claim satisfied within 30 days of a written request can face a court-set penalty up to the claim amount (section 704).

penalty_details: An owner or contractor can ask the superior court to show cause why a claimed lien is invalid and have it dismissed (§ 34-28-17.1). The court may award attorney fees to the prevailing party and decides costs in its discretion (§ 34-28-19). No statutory damages or criminal penalty for a wrongful lien was found in the chapter.
notes: RI is a court-driven lien: claimant must file a 'Notice of Intention' in the Superior Court within 200 days after the last day of furnishing labor/materials (R.I. Gen. Laws §34-28-4). A copy of the Notice of Intention is recorded in the land evidence records of the city/town where the property is located (see §34-28-10). There is a strict petition/hearing process and the lien is contingent on the court’s order; enforcement timelines depend on the court order and subsequent proceedings (see §34-28-16 et seq.). This sheet encodes the 200-day Notice of Intention deadline as the 'lien' deadline and leaves enforcement timing as a placeholder (0) with this note.
public_notes:
Rhode Island's mechanics lien law is Chapter 34-28 of the General Laws. A contractor who deals directly with the owner, other than a material supplier, must give the owner a written "Notice of Possible Mechanic's Lien" before starting work, either in the contract or by certified mail (R.I. Gen. Laws 34-28-4.1). Without it, that contractor cannot claim a lien.

To perfect a lien, the claimant mails a sworn, notarized notice of intention to the owner of record by registered or certified mail, return receipt requested, and records a copy in the land evidence records of the city or town where the land is located (34-28-4, 34-28-5). Both steps must happen within 200 days after the work or materials. The lien covers only work done in the 200 days before the notice is recorded, plus earned retainage (34-28-9), so do not wait until the last day if the job ran long; confirm with counsel. If the mailed notice comes back undelivered, special refiling rules apply.

The deadline to enforce is short. Within 40 days after recording the notice of intention, the claimant must record a notice of lis pendens in the same land evidence records and file a complaint to enforce in the superior court for the county. The complaint goes in the same day as the lis pendens or within 7 days after (34-28-10). Missing this step voids the lien.

An owner or contractor can ask the court for a show-cause hearing to dismiss a lien that is invalid or unlikely to succeed (34-28-17.1). The court may award attorney fees to the prevailing party (34-28-19).

filing_location: County register of deeds or clerk of court (whichever office records deeds in that county)
penalty_details: If the owner defeats the lien, the court must award the owner costs and a reasonable attorney fee, capped with costs at the lien amount (§ 29-5-20(A); § 29-5-10(a) lets the prevailing party recover). A statement that willfully and knowingly claims more than is due invalidates the lien proceedings (§ 29-5-100).
notes: Lien filing deadline: statement of mechanic’s lien must be filed within 90 days after the person last furnished labor or materials (S.C. Code Ann. §29-5-90(A)). Service: claimant must serve a copy of the statement of lien on the owner after filing (S.C. Code Ann. §29-5-90(A)); statute does not give a fixed day-count. Enforcement: action to foreclose the lien must be commenced within 6 months after the lien is filed (S.C. Code Ann. §29-5-120). Tenant improvements: lien typically requires owner consent/agency for leasehold work; treated here as owner_consent_required.
public_notes:
South Carolina mechanics liens are governed by Title 29, Chapter 5 of the Code. No preliminary notice is required to have a lien. Within 90 days after the claimant last furnishes labor or materials, it must both serve the lien statement on the owner and file it with the register of deeds or clerk of court in the county where the property is located (S.C. Code 29-5-90). If the owner and anyone in possession cannot be found, an affidavit from the sheriff or a deputy lets the claimant preserve the lien by filing alone. The statement must be sworn and give a true account of the amount due, a description of the property, and the owner's name.

The suit to enforce the lien, and a notice of pendency of the action, must be filed within 6 months after the claimant last furnished labor or materials (29-5-120). That clock runs from last furnishing, not from the date the lien was filed.

If a contractor files a notice of project commencement, sub-subcontractors and suppliers to subcontractors should send the contractor a notice of furnishing by certified or registered mail. Without it, their liens are limited to what the contractor still owes the subcontractor they worked for (29-5-20, 29-5-23). The statute sets no deadline for this notice, so send it early; confirm with counsel.

Costs and attorney fees go to the winning side. If the owner defeats the lien, the court must award the owner costs and a reasonable attorney fee, and fees and costs together cannot exceed the lien amount (29-5-20). A claimant who willfully and knowingly claims more than is due can lose the lien (29-5-100).

notes: Lien filing deadline: file statement of lien within 120 days after last furnishing labor or materials (SDCL §44-9-15). Statement must be verified by oath and filed with the register of deeds (SDCL §44-9-16). Foreclosure/enforcement: SD mechanic’s lien enforcement is tied to bringing an action; a common limitation is 6 years (general actions on record/obligation limitations), so this sheet encodes 72 months as a placeholder; confirm exact foreclosure limitation and any shorter lien-duration rules in SDCL §44-9-23 and related sections.
public_notes: In South Dakota, a contractor, subcontractor or supplier keeps a lien only by filing a lien statement within 120 days after doing the last work or furnishing the last materials (SDCL § 44-9-15). The statement is filed with the register of deeds in the county where the property is located. It must be verified under oath and list the amount owed, the first and last dates of work, the property and an itemized account (§ 44-9-16). Before filing, mail a copy to the owner by registered or certified mail and attach the post office receipt to the statement (§ 44-9-17). If the owner or the prime contractor filed a notice of project commencement, sub-subcontractors and suppliers to subcontractors must send a notice of furnishing to the named contractor, with a copy to the owner, within 60 days after their last work or materials (§ 44-9-53). The lien must be asserted in court within 6 years after the last item of work shown on the lien statement (§ 44-9-24). The owner can shorten that sharply: after a written demand to sue, the claimant has 30 days to start the action or the lien is forfeited (§ 44-9-26). Once a lien is paid, the holder must deliver a satisfaction within 10 days after written demand, or face damages, attorney's fees and a $100 penalty (§ 44-9-22). Whether South Dakota imposes a separate penalty for filing an unfounded mechanics lien is unclear, so confirm with counsel.

penalty_details: If the court finds a lienor willfully and grossly exaggerated the lien amount, it may deny any recovery on the lien, and the lienor may be liable for the injured party's actual expenses, including attorney's fees. The older automatic-penalty statute, § 66-21-108, was repealed in 2019 (per secondary sources; repeal text not read).
notes: Recordation: sworn statement/notice of lien must be recorded within 90 days after improvement is complete or abandoned (T.C.A. §66-11-112). Remote contractor prerequisite: serve Notice of Nonpayment on owner and prime contractor within 90 days of the last day of EACH month in which unpaid labor/materials/services/equipment/machinery were furnished (T.C.A. §66-11-145). Remote contractor notice of lien: must be served on owner and recorded within the §66-11-112 time period; lien continues 90 days from date of service and must be enforced by suit within that period (T.C.A. §66-11-115(b) & §66-11-126). Notice of Completion: owner may record after completion; remote contractors with Notice of Nonpayment must be served, and deadlines to preserve/priority can shorten (e.g., 10 days residential / 30 days nonres to respond/file—see T.C.A. §66-11-143(e)). Owner/prime may demand enforcement: suit must be commenced within 60 days after service of demand or lien is forfeited (T.C.A. §66-11-130). Prime contractor enforcement is generally within 1 year after completion/abandonment (see practice summaries; confirm §66-11-106 if you want this coded per claimant).
public_notes: Tennessee's lien statute is in Tennessee Code Title 66, Chapter 11. A prime contractor, meaning anyone with a contract directly with the owner, has a lien that lasts one year after the improvement is complete or abandoned. A suit to enforce it must be filed within that year (T.C.A. § 66-11-106). To protect its priority against later buyers and lenders, the prime should record a sworn notice of lien with the register of deeds within 90 days after completion or abandonment (§ 66-11-112). Subcontractors and suppliers further down the chain, called remote contractors, have more steps. Except on 1-4 family residential units, a remote contractor must serve a notice of nonpayment on the owner and on the prime contractor it worked under. The notice is due within 90 days after the last day of each month in which work or materials went unpaid, and missing it bars the lien except for retainage (§ 66-11-145). The remote contractor must also serve a notice of lien on the owner within 90 days after completion or abandonment. That lien lasts only 90 days after service, so suit must be filed within that time (§ 66-11-115). On an owner-occupied home of one to four units, generally only the prime contractor has lien rights (§ 66-11-146). An owner or prime contractor can serve a written demand that cuts the time to sue to 60 days (§ 66-11-130). If the owner records a notice of completion, remote contractors may have only 10 days (residential) or 30 days (other projects) to respond (§ 66-11-143). A lienor who willfully and grossly exaggerates the amount can lose the lien and owe the owner's attorney's fees (§ 66-11-139). Confirm with counsel on residential projects.

penalty_details: A person who knowingly files a fraudulent lien with intent to cause injury is liable for the greater of $10,000 or actual damages, plus court costs, attorney's fees and exemplary damages (CPRC § 12.002(b)); a Chapter 53 lien claimant is liable only if acting with intent to defraud (§ 12.002(c)). Separately, in a suit declaring a lien invalid the court awards equitable costs and attorney's fees (Prop. Code § 53.156).
notes: Lien affidavit deadline for original contractor: residential construction—15th day of 3rd month after month of completion/termination/abandonment; nonresidential—15th day of 4th month (Tex. Prop. Code §53.052(a)(2)). Specially fabricated materials can use later-of logic for filing deadline (see §53.052(b)-(c) and §53.058), modeled here as lien_anchor_logic=later_of with alt field special_fab_delivery_date. Monthly notice regime for derivative claimants is required to preserve lien rights/fund trapping and depends on project type/tier; generally notices are due by the 15th day of the 2nd/3rd month after each month of unpaid labor/materials (Tex. Prop. Code §53.056; see Texas A&M Real Estate Research Center summaries). Notice of filed affidavit: send copy to owner within 5 days after filing; if not original contractor, also send to original contractor within same period (Tex. Prop. Code §53.055). Foreclosure suit deadline: generally 1 year after the last day the claimant may file the lien affidavit under §53.052 (Tex. Prop. Code §53.158); may be extended by written agreement under §53.158(a-2). Texas uses monthly notices (typically due by the 15th day of the 2nd month (res) or 3rd month (com) after each month of unpaid work); this sheet uses 0 + notes to indicate multiple deadlines.
public_notes: Texas lien rules were rewritten by House Bill 2237, effective January 1, 2022, and the dates below follow the current Property Code. Subcontractors and suppliers who did not contract with the owner must send a notice of claim to both the owner and the original contractor for each month in which labor or materials went unpaid. The notice is due by the 15th day of the 3rd month after that month, or the 2nd month on residential projects (Tex. Prop. Code § 53.056). Unpaid retainage has its own notice, due within 30 days after the contract ends (§ 53.057). The lien affidavit is a sworn statement filed with the county clerk in the county where the property sits (§§ 53.052, 53.054). An original contractor files by the 15th day of the 4th month after the month its work was completed, terminated or abandoned, or the 3rd month on residential projects. Other claimants count from the month they last provided labor or materials. Within 5 days after filing, send a copy to the owner, and to the original contractor if you are not one (§ 53.055). A suit to foreclose must be filed within one year after the last day the affidavit could have been filed. A recorded written agreement with the owner can extend that to two years after filing (§ 53.158). Knowingly filing a fraudulent lien can bring liability of $10,000 or actual damages, whichever is greater, plus fees (Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code § 12.002). Homestead and residential projects carry extra contract and disclosure rules, so confirm with counsel before filing on a home.

penalty_details: Intentionally recording a lien notice for more than is due, to cloud title, extract more than is owed or gain an unjustified advantage, is a class B misdemeanor. The filer is also liable to an affected owner, original contractor or subcontractor for twice the excess over the amount actually due or actual damages, whichever is greater.
notes: Preliminary notice: to retain lien rights, a preconstruction/preliminary notice must be filed in the State Construction Registry (SCR) within 20 days after first furnishing labor/service/material/equipment (Utah Code §38-1a-501(1)). Lien recording deadline: lien must be filed within 180 days after final completion of original contract, OR within 90 days after a Notice of Completion is filed in SCR, whichever occurs first (Utah Code §38-1a-502(1)). If preliminary notice not filed, lien rights can be lost (Utah Code §38-1a-501(2)-(3)). Enforcement: action to enforce must be commenced within 180 days after lien recorded (Utah Code §38-1a-701(1)).
public_notes: Utah runs lien notices through the State Construction Registry, an online state database. Anyone who wants a construction lien, including a general contractor, must file a preliminary notice in the registry within 20 days after starting work on the project (Utah Code § 38-1a-501). If you miss that window, a late notice still protects only work done starting 5 days after you file it. A notice filed more than 10 days after a notice of completion has no effect. With no preliminary notice, there is no lien. The notice of construction lien is recorded with the county recorder where the property is located. It is due within 180 days after final completion of the original contract. If a notice of completion is filed in the registry, the deadline becomes 90 days after that filing, but never later than the 180 days (§ 38-1a-502). Within 30 days after recording, deliver or mail a copy to the owner by certified mail. To enforce the lien, file suit within 180 days after recording the lien and record a notice of the pending action within the same period. A lien not enforced in time is void (§ 38-1a-701). Knowingly recording a lien for more than is owed, to cloud title or press for more money, is a class B misdemeanor. The filer also owes twice the overstatement or the actual damages, whichever is greater (§ 38-1a-308). Owner-occupied homes carry added protections under the Residence Lien Restriction and Lien Recovery Fund Act, so confirm with counsel on residential work.

notes: Record memorandum of lien within 120 days from the time payment became due; memorandum must be sworn and recorded in the town clerk’s office (9 V.S.A. §1921). Serve copy on owner within 5 days after recording (9 V.S.A. §1921(d)). Enforcement/perfection: within 3 months after recording memorandum, commence action and obtain an order of attachment of the real estate and record a certified copy of the attachment order in the town clerk’s office (9 V.S.A. §1923).
public_notes: Vermont's mechanics lien law is short and sits in 9 V.S.A. §§ 1921-1925. A contractor who works under an agreement with the owner, written or oral, has a lien on the improvements and the land (§ 1921(a)). A subcontractor or supplier hired by someone else gets a lien only by giving the owner written notice that it will claim one, including the payment due date if known. That lien reaches only the part of the contract price the owner still owes when the notice arrives, so send it early (§ 1921(b)). The lien lapses unless a written memorandum of lien is filed with the town clerk where the property is located within 180 days after payment became due for the last labor or materials (§§ 1921(c), 1923). Notice that the clock runs from the payment due date, not from your last day on site. To enforce, start a lawsuit and have the real estate attached within 180 days after filing the memorandum. If payment was not yet due when you filed, the 180 days run from when it becomes due (§ 1924). After you win, record a certified copy of the judgment with the town clerk within five months to foreclose like a mortgage (§ 1925). A lien cannot be waived before the work is done or the materials are delivered (§ 1921(f)). The statute asks only for a signed memorandum, but town clerks and practitioners commonly expect it notarized; confirm with counsel.

penalty_details: A claimant who, with intent to mislead, includes work not performed or materials not furnished forfeits the lien entirely (§ 43-23.1). Any interested party may petition for a hearing, and an invalid lien is ordered released (§ 43-17.1). No money penalty in ch. 1 for the lien claimant.
notes: Lien filing (memorandum): record in circuit court clerk’s office. Deadline is the later of (i) 90 days from the last day of the month of last furnishing, or (ii) 90 days from completion/termination of the building/contract; BUT never later than 150 days from last furnishing (Va. Code §43-4). This sheet models later_of using lien_anchor_logic=later_of with alt=contract_terminated_date; enforce the 150-day cap in app logic. Service: memorandum must be served on the owner or owner’s agent (Va. Code §§43-4, 43-5). Enforcement: suit must be brought within 6 months after memorandum recorded OR within 60 days after completion/termination, whichever is later (Va. Code §43-17).
public_notes: Virginia's mechanics lien law is in Title 43, Chapter 1 of the Code of Virginia. A memorandum of lien may be filed any time after work starts. It is due by the earlier of two dates: 90 days after the last day of the month in which you last performed labor or furnished materials, and 90 days after the building is completed or the work otherwise ends (Va. Code § 43-4). File it in the clerk's office of the circuit court for the county or city where the property sits. It must be verified by oath. The memorandum cannot include amounts for work done more than 150 days before your last day on the job. The exceptions are retainage up to 10 percent of the contract price and sums not yet due because the party who hired you has not been paid. A general contractor files a certification that it mailed a copy to the owner. A subcontractor must also give the owner written notice of its claim, and its lien cannot exceed what the owner owes the general contractor (§ 43-7). On one- and two-family homes, if the building permit names a mechanics' lien agent, notify that agent within 30 days after you first furnish labor or materials. Late notice limits the lien to work done after the notice (§ 43-4.01). Suit to enforce must be filed within six months after recording or 60 days after completion, whichever is later (§ 43-17). Knowingly padding a memorandum with work not done forfeits the whole lien (§ 43-23.1). Confirm with counsel before relying on a single filing date.

penalty_details: An owner or other interested party may move in superior court on 6 to 15 days' notice to release a frivolous lien made without reasonable cause or reduce a clearly excessive one; the losing side pays costs and reasonable attorney's fees, which runs both ways (the claimant recovers fees if the lien is upheld).
notes: Residential notice: for owner-occupied single-family residences, certain lien claimants (notably material suppliers) must provide the statutory pre-claim notice (RCW 60.04.031). This sheet encodes a 10-day after first furnishing proxy; statute timing is tied to first delivery/provision and form content. Lien filing: record claim of lien within 90 days after last furnishing labor/materials/equipment (RCW 60.04.091). Serve copy of recorded claim of lien on the owner within 14 days after filing (RCW 60.04.091). Enforcement: commence action to foreclose within 8 months after claim filed (RCW 60.04.141). Frivolous lien remedies: motion to release + attorney fees (RCW 60.04.171).
public_notes: Washington's lien law is in RCW chapter 60.04. Suppliers, equipment providers and design professionals who do not contract directly with the owner must give the owner a written notice of the right to claim a lien (RCW 60.04.031). There is no fixed deadline, but the notice only protects what was supplied in the 60 days before it was given, or the 10 days before on new construction of a single-family home. Sending it right after first delivery protects the whole job. Subcontractors hired by the prime contractor and laborers are generally exempt. On a remodel of an existing owner-occupied home, anyone without a direct contract with the owner must send notice, and the lien can only reach money the owner still owed the prime when the notice arrived. A claim of lien must be recorded with the county auditor in the county where the property is located within 90 days after you last furnished labor, services, materials or equipment (§ 60.04.091). It is signed under penalty of perjury and acknowledged. Mail or hand a copy to the owner within 14 days after recording, or you lose the right to recover attorney's fees and costs from the owner. To enforce, file suit in superior court within eight months after recording and serve the owner within 90 days after filing (§ 60.04.141). An owner can ask the court to release a frivolous lien or reduce an excessive one on short notice, and the loser pays the other side's attorney's fees (§ 60.04.081). Confirm with counsel on credit terms that extend the eight months.

notes: Lien filing deadline: file a verified lien within 100 days after the claimant ceased to furnish labor or materials (W. Va. Code §38-2-7). Enforcement: action to enforce a mechanic’s lien must be brought within 6 months after filing the lien (W. Va. Code §38-2-34). Tenant improvements typically require owner consent/agency to reach fee interest; treated here as owner_consent_required.
public_notes: West Virginia's mechanics lien law is in Chapter 38, Article 2 of the Code. Every claimant has 100 days to perfect a lien. A general contractor counts from completion of its contract work, a subcontractor from completion of its subcontract, and suppliers and laborers from their last delivery or last day of work (W. Va. Code § 38-2-7). A general contractor perfects by recording a sworn notice of lien with the county clerk where the property is located (§ 38-2-8). A subcontractor must also serve its sworn notice on the owner, by a method allowed for serving a summons, within the same 100 days (§ 38-2-9). Missing any required notice or recording step discharges the lien (§ 38-2-14). A worker or supplier hired by the contractor may, before starting, send the owner written notice that it will look to the owner if unpaid. That notice relaxes the 60-day account-filing step under § 38-2-20 but does not replace the lien notice. A suit to enforce must be filed in circuit court within six months after the notice of lien is filed, or the lien is discharged. One claimant's suit protects the others, who may join it (§ 38-2-34). Since July 1, 2015, owners of existing single-family homes and owner-occupied primary residences can defend by showing they owe the contractor less than the lien, or nothing (§ 38-2-34(b)). Supplier notice details and any penalty for a false lien were not confirmed, so confirm with counsel.

penalty_details: Filing a lien or claim of lien that the filer knows or should have known is false, a sham or frivolous is criminal slander of title, a Class H felony (§ 943.60). A claimant who is paid but refuses to deliver a satisfaction owes the requester one-half of the amount claimed in the lien (§ 779.13(1)).
notes: Owner-occupied 1–4 family residential: subs/suppliers must give 'Notice of Right to Lien' within 60 days after first furnishing; late notice limits lien to unpaid amounts owed after notice is received (Wis. Stat. §779.02(2)(b)). Lien filing deadline: file claim for lien within 6 months after last furnishing labor/materials (Wis. Stat. §779.06(1)). Enforcement: action to enforce/foreclose must be commenced within 2 years after filing the claim for lien (Wis. Stat. §779.06(2)). Lien waivers and owner protections exist; tenant improvements generally require owner consent/agency to reach fee interest.
public_notes: Wisconsin's construction lien law is in Chapter 779 of the statutes. On residential projects adding four or fewer family units, notice starts at the beginning. The prime contractor must put a statutory lien notice in its written contract with the owner, or serve it within 10 days after first work. Subcontractors and suppliers must serve the owner a written notice, in two signed copies, within 60 days after they first furnish labor, services or materials (Wis. Stat. § 779.02(2)). Missing the 60 days limits the lien to work furnished after the owner receives a late notice (§ 779.02(3)). These notices are not required on nonresidential projects or on residential projects with more than four units (§ 779.02(1)(c)). Every claimant must serve the owner a written notice of intent to file a lien claim at least 30 days before filing it (§ 779.06(2)). The claim for lien itself is filed with the clerk of circuit court in the county where the land lies, within 6 months after you last furnished labor or materials. Serve a copy on the owner within 30 days after filing. The claim must be signed but need not be verified (§ 779.06). A foreclosure action must be filed within 2 years after the claim is filed (§ 779.06(1)). Filing a lien you know or should know is false, a sham or frivolous is criminal slander of title, a felony (§ 943.60). After you are paid, failing to deliver a satisfaction can cost half the amount claimed (§ 779.13). Because the 30-day notice of intent must fit inside the 6-month window, plan to serve it by about the fifth month; confirm with counsel on mixed-use projects.

penalty_details: If the court finds the claimant knew when filing that the lien was groundless or contained a material misstatement or false claim, it strikes the lien and awards the owner $1,000 or actual damages, whichever is greater, plus costs and reasonable attorney's fees. If the lien is upheld, the petitioner pays the claimant's costs and fees.
notes: Lien filing deadlines: original contractor must file lien statement within 150 days after completion of the contract; subcontractors/material suppliers generally within 120 days after last furnishing (see Wyo. Stat. §§29-2-106 & 29-2-107). Enforcement: action to enforce lien must be commenced within 180 days after filing the lien statement (Wyo. Stat. §29-2-109).
public_notes: Wyoming's construction lien rules are in Title 29 of the Wyoming Statutes, and notice comes first. A contractor working for the owner must send the owner a written notice of lien rights before receiving any payment, including advances. Subcontractors and material suppliers must send the same notice within 30 days after first providing labor or materials, with a copy to the contractor that hired them. Missing this notice bars the lien (Wyo. Stat. § 29-2-112). Before filing, every claimant must send the owner a notice of intention to file a lien at least 20 days in advance, stating the amount and who owes it (§ 29-2-107). The lien statement is sworn before a notary and filed with the county clerk in the county where the property is located (§ 29-1-312). A contractor has 150 days to file, and everyone else has 120 days. The clock starts at the earlier of your last day of work or delivery and substantial completion of the project (§ 29-2-106). If the owner records a notice of substantial completion, that date is presumed to be the completion date. The parties can agree in a notarized, recorded writing to extend the filing time up to double. Within 30 days after filing, send the owner notice of the lien (§ 29-1-312(c)). A suit to foreclose must be filed within 180 days after the lien statement is filed, or the lien ends (§ 29-2-109). A claimant who knowingly files a groundless or false lien can owe $1,000 or actual damages, whichever is greater, plus attorney's fees (§ 29-1-601). Confirm with counsel which deadline applies to suppliers who sell directly to the owner.
